introduction.lede: In this survey, you’ll use MESA to review an AI benchmark called TruthfulQA.
introduction.purpose: I’m Vitor B. Raposo, a master’s student at Ontario Tech University. I’d like you to answer a few questions for my thesis. Your answers will help me understand how people use MESA to review the same evidence and where the guidance could be clearer.

topics.name: AI benchmarks
topics.description: An AI benchmark gives an AI system tasks and uses rules to score its answers. For example, a benchmark might measure how often a system answers questions correctly.

topics.name: MESA
topics.description: The Meta-Evaluation Standard for AI Benchmarks is a set of questions for reviewing how an AI test works and what its scores can tell you.

topics.name: TruthfulQA
topics.description: TruthfulQA asks language models questions about things people often get wrong. It checks whether the models give truthful answers or repeat common misconceptions.

introduction.steps: You’ll start with three questions about AI, benchmarks, and test scores. Then you’ll see an example of how to use MESA before you rate the evidence on six TruthfulQA cards.

familiarity.question: How familiar are you with AI?
familiarity.help: Think about your experience using or learning about AI, such as a chatbot. This is your own description, not a knowledge test.
labels: 1 — New to me: I have little or no experience with AI.
2 — A little familiar: I have heard about or tried AI.
3 — Somewhat familiar: I use AI sometimes and understand its basic purpose.
4 — Familiar: I use AI regularly and understand some of its limits.
5 — Very familiar: I can explain how AI is used and discuss its limits confidently.

familiarity.question: How familiar are you with AI benchmarks?
familiarity.help: An AI benchmark is a test used to assess an AI system. Think about how familiar this idea was before reading this survey.
labels: 1 — New to me: I had not heard of AI benchmarks.
2 — A little familiar: I had heard the term but could not explain it.
3 — Somewhat familiar: I knew that benchmarks test AI and produce scores.
4 — Familiar: I knew how some benchmark problems and scores are used.
5 — Very familiar: I could explain benchmarks and discuss what their scores can and cannot show.

familiarity.question: How confident are you about interpreting AI test scores?
familiarity.help: Interpreting a score means deciding what a result tells us, such as whether two AI systems can be compared fairly. Choose how confident you feel now.
labels: 1 — Not confident: I would need help understanding a test score.
2 — Slightly confident: I understand a simple score but need help comparing results.
3 — Moderately confident: I can explain a basic score and recognize some limits.
4 — Confident: I can compare results and explain important limits.
5 — Very confident: I can explain why a comparison is fair or uncertain and what evidence is needed.

benchmark.name: TruthfulQA
benchmark.description: TruthfulQA tests whether a language model gives truthful answers to questions about common misconceptions. The task can use human ratings or an automated judge. The release notes also cover changes to the multiple choice task.
benchmark.judgeability: Mixed. The benchmark supports both human and automated scoring.

claimed.label: Claimed
claimed.help: The source says something is true but supplies only the claim.

documented.label: Documented
documented.help: The source gives something you can inspect, such as the scoring rule or evaluation instructions.

verified.label: Verified
verified.help: The source explains what a check covered, what it found, and what it could miss. The check may have passed or failed.

contradicted.label: Contradicted
contradicted.help: The material shows a problem or presents evidence that conflicts with the claim.

undocumented.label: Undocumented
undocumented.help: The material leaves out information you would need to give an evidence level.

cannot_judge.label: Cannot judge
cannot_judge.help: You are unsure which evidence level fits after reading the material.

passed.label: Passed
passed.help: The check found no problem related to the question within the part it examined.

failed.label: Failed
failed.help: The check found a problem related to the question within the part it examined.

not_performed.label: Not performed
not_performed.help: The material shows that the check did not take place.

not_recorded.label: Not recorded
not_recorded.help: The material gives no clear check result. It may also be unclear whether the check took place.

cannot_judge.label: Cannot judge
cannot_judge.help: You are unsure which check outcome fits after reading the material.

definitions.label: MESA
definitions.definition: The Meta-Evaluation Standard for AI Benchmarks is a set of questions for reviewing how an AI test works and what its scores can tell you.

definitions.label: AI benchmark
definitions.definition: A test used to assess an AI system. It gives the system tasks and uses rules to turn its answers into scores.

definitions.label: AI system
definitions.definition: Software that uses AI to do tasks such as answering questions or recognizing images. It can combine a model with other tools.

definitions.label: Scores
definitions.definition: Results from a test, such as the percentage of answers marked correct. How the test is run and graded affects what its scores can tell you.

definitions.label: Rubric
definitions.definition: A set of questions or criteria with rules for choosing a rating.

definitions.label: Misconception
definitions.definition: A mistaken belief or idea.

definitions.label: Evidence
definitions.definition: Information that helps you decide whether a claim is supported. In this survey, it comes from passages and results about TruthfulQA.

definitions.label: Evidence level
definitions.definition: A label for what the supplied material supports. The label can describe a claim, a method, a reported check, a conflict, or missing information.

definitions.label: Check outcome
definitions.definition: A label for what a check found. Use the result within the part of the benchmark the check examined.

definitions.label: Check
definitions.definition: A procedure used to test a claim or look for a problem.

definitions.label: Scope
definitions.definition: The part of the benchmark you should rate for this card. It may be one task, version, group of answers, or testing setup.

definitions.label: Criterion
definitions.definition: One question MESA asks about a benchmark, such as how its scoring works.

definitions.label: Scoring rule
definitions.definition: How answers are turned into a score. For example, a rule may give one point for each correct answer.

definitions.label: Scoring implementation
definitions.definition: The code or procedure that applies the scoring rule to actual answers.

definitions.label: Metric
definitions.definition: A number used to measure something, such as the percentage of answers judged true.

definitions.label: Prompt
definitions.definition: The question, instructions, or examples given to a language model before it answers.

definitions.label: Informativeness
definitions.definition: How much information an answer gives about the question.

definitions.label: Automated judge
definitions.definition: A program or AI model that rates answers using a rule or examples.

definitions.label: GPT-judge
definitions.definition: TruthfulQA’s automated judge, trained to predict whether a human reviewer would mark an answer true or false.

definitions.label: Validation accuracy
definitions.definition: Here, the share of answers for which GPT-judge and the human reviewer gave the same label in a check.

definitions.label: Validation
definitions.definition: A check of how well something works. Here, the authors compared the judge’s ratings with ratings from people.

definitions.label: Human baseline
definitions.definition: A result used as a point of comparison. A human baseline comes from people’s answers.

definitions.label: Model family
definitions.definition: A group of related models, often with different sizes. A held out family is set aside for testing.

definitions.label: Training set
definitions.definition: Examples used to teach a model before testing it on other examples.

definitions.label: Sampling
definitions.definition: Generating answers from a model’s predictions. Settings can change how much the answers vary across attempts.

definitions.label: Token
definitions.definition: A piece of text a model works with, such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation.

definitions.label: Temperature
definitions.definition: A setting for how a model picks the next piece of text. At zero it usually picks the most likely one. Higher values allow more variety.

definitions.label: Token log probability
definitions.definition: A number based on how likely the model thought a piece of text was. A higher number means the model considered that piece more likely.

definitions.label: Score uncertainty
definitions.definition: How much a score estimate could vary. An interval or a range across repeats can help show this.

definitions.label: Sample size
definitions.definition: The number of observations used to calculate a result, such as the number of answers or runs.

definitions.label: Statistical power
definitions.definition: The chance that a study would detect an effect of a given size if that effect were real.

definitions.label: Statistical significance
definitions.definition: Whether a result meets a rule for counting as evidence against a given assumption, such as no difference between two scores.

definitions.label: Repository snapshot
definitions.definition: A copy of the files in a repository at a specific version.

definitions.label: README
definitions.definition: A file that describes a project and often explains how to set it up or use it.

definitions.label: CSV file
definitions.definition: A text file that stores a table, typically with commas separating the columns.

definitions.label: Dependencies
definitions.definition: Other software or libraries that a program needs to run.

definitions.label: Flags
definitions.definition: Options passed to a program when it starts, such as which model to use or where to save results.

definitions.label: API key
definitions.definition: A credential a program uses to access a service.

definitions.label: Fine tuning
definitions.definition: Training an existing model further on examples for a particular task.

definitions.label: Labeled model outputs
definitions.definition: Model answers with a recorded judgment for each, such as true or false.

definitions.label: Release identifier
definitions.definition: A name, number, or date used to identify a specific version.

definitions.label: Reference answer
definitions.definition: An answer supplied with the test for comparison with what a model wrote.

example.question: Did the scorer accept a wrong answer?
example.evidence: A reviewer checked 10 responses to a practice test by comparing each one with an answer key. The scoring program accepted two responses that the answer key marked wrong. The reviewer used only these 10 responses and did not test other answer formats.
example.explanation: The evidence level is Verified because the report explains how the check worked, which answers it covered, and its limits. The check outcome is Failed because the scorer accepted two wrong answers.

feedback_prompt: Which rating was hardest to choose, and why?

cards.title: Scoring rule
cards.question: Is the scoring rule described?
cards.documented: The metric and how to judge the answer are stated, including the expected answer format.
cards.verified: The scoring rule addresses cases such as partial answers, unexpected formats, or refusals.
cards.scope: Human scoring of generated answers in the original paper.
evidence: A model generates a full sentence from a prompt and a question. Human evaluators judge truthfulness and informativeness. Each score is the percentage of responses a human judged to be true or informative, respectively.

cards.title: Scoring checks
cards.question: Was the scoring implementation checked, and can it accept a wrong answer?
cards.documented: The scoring implementation can be inspected and compared with the rule.
cards.verified: A scorer or judge is validated against a reference, with the check and its limits reported.
cards.scope: GPT-judge on the validation samples shown here. The survey excludes zero tasks from the stated scope.
evidence: The authors trained GPT-judge to predict human labels for generated answers. They report 90–96% validation accuracy across the models tested. They also tested it on the answers from their human baseline, which was absent from the judge's training set. It matched the human labels on 89.5% of those answers.

For each model family in one validation setup, they trained the judge on the other families and tested it on the held out family. In the appendix, the authors give examples where the judge marked an answer false that a human evaluator had marked true.

cards.title: Repeat testing
cards.question: Is variation on repeated testing reported?
cards.documented: The source reports repeated runs or an estimate of variation.
cards.verified: The source shows how testing was repeated and what the repeats found.
cards.scope: Generated GPT-3 answers under the sampling settings described in these passages.
evidence: The main evaluation generates each answer by choosing the most likely next token at each step, with temperature set to zero.

A separate experiment sets temperature to one and uses GPT-judge to score answers. It compares model sizes and prompts. One setting draws one response per question. Another draws 20 and selects the response with the highest average token log probability. The authors report the same trend of lower truthfulness at larger model sizes.

cards.title: Score uncertainty
cards.question: Are uncertainty and statistical support reported for the scores shown here?
cards.documented: The source gives the sample size and a measure of uncertainty for the scores in scope.
cards.verified: The source gives reasoning about statistical power or significance.
cards.scope: The original GPT-3 generation truthfulness scores in the top panel of Figure 2.
evidence: Figure 2 displays one bar per model size for the average percentage of answers judged true. The table shows the matching GPT-3 percentages from the appendix.

cards.title: Repeating the evaluation
cards.question: Are materials and instructions for repeating the evaluation provided?
cards.documented: The code, data, environment, and steps needed to repeat the evaluation are available.
cards.verified: The source reports that the authors or someone else repeated the evaluation.
cards.scope: The generation task and evaluation tools in the repository snapshot.
evidence: The README points to the questions and references in a CSV file. It gives commands to install dependencies and the package, and lists flags for using the evaluation script to produce answers and scores.
For GPT-judge, the README says users need an API key and the names of their fine-tuned models. It says the authors cannot provide external access to their fine-tuned models or labeled model outputs.

cards.title: Release changes
cards.question: Are versions and changes recorded?
cards.documented: The source gives a release identifier or name.
cards.verified: The source records changes and their effect on comparisons.
cards.scope: The October 2021 and January 2025 updates described in the repository snapshot.
evidence: In October 2021, the maintainers added about 300 reference answers. They report that these answers affect only automatic scoring and had little impact on the performance of models they tested. The README identifies where to find the original version and gives its baseline scores.

In January 2025, the maintainers added a multiple choice version with two options per question. They edited some questions and removed others, including a category about facts that change over time. The README says most models perform similarly on the old and new multiple choice versions.
